## Chapter 50: Analysis of Variance (One-Way ANOVA)

### Getting Ready for a One-Way ANOVA

The way a Six Sigma practitioner approaches a one-way ANOVA is very similar to how they'd approach any other hypothesis test. First, you start with a real-world problem — a practical or business problem. In the example above, that problem is whether there's variation in customer satisfaction across a restaurant chain's various locations.

As with any hypothesis test, you need a null hypothesis and an alternative. The null hypothesis is that there's no difference between the sample means.

μ1 = μ2 = ... = μx

The alternative hypothesis is that at least one of the means isn't statistically equal.

After stating the null and alternative hypotheses, a Six Sigma practitioner should check whether any assumptions within the model are appropriate. That includes assumptions about errors, as well as some basic assumptions about the ANOVA model.

First, the samples used for the ANOVA need to be randomly selected. Remember, that's always a necessary assumption for inferential statistics.

> **Between-Sample versus Within-Sample Variance**
>
> ANOVA calculations compare between-sample variance with within-sample variance. Between-sample variance is the variance that occurs across all the samples being analyzed. Within-sample variance is the variance that occurs within a single sample or group.
>
> The reason this distinction matters is that within-sample variance obviously affects between-sample variance. If you're dealing with five separate samples and each sample has large variance, then the variance between the samples is likely to be large too. Part of the ANOVA calculation compares between-sample variance to determine whether it's large enough relative to within-sample variance to indicate a statistical difference.
>

After making sure the samples are randomly selected, Six Sigma practitioners need to validate six other assumptions about the data before running a one-way ANOVA test.

1. The dependent variable, or outcome, needs to be continuous in nature. That means it's a ratio or an interval. In the earlier examples, the dependent variable included the customer satisfaction score (numeric), the number of calls answered per day, and the cycle time for a given outcome. All of these are examples of continuous data. Anything that can be measured in time, temperature, feet and inches (or centimeters and meters), money, or ratios is typically continuous in nature.
2. The list of independent variables contains two or more unrelated groups or categories. Teams A, B, and C are three independent variables. If you're measuring the performance of five different workers, then you might have five independent variables. In the restaurant example, the five different restaurants are independent variables. Categorical variables can include people, times, shifts, teams, departments, locations, various demographic groups (age, gender, ethnicity), or occupations.
3. The observations are independent. First, you need to make sure there are no dependencies within groups. If you're measuring the performance of three different teams in a department, but several employees work across multiple teams, then the results aren't fully independent. Second, you need to make sure the observations within groups aren't dependent.
4. There are no significant outliers in your data. Outliers skew the accuracy of a one-way ANOVA, but you don't need to scrap the entire test because of a single explainable outlier. As a Six Sigma practitioner, you need to review your data, investigate outliers, and discard them appropriately. For example, if a Six Sigma practitioner is reviewing response times for customer emails, they might review data samples from nine different employees. One employee's data includes three outliers where emails were answered after a much longer time than every other sample indicates. The Six Sigma practitioner can investigate this and note that the employee in question was on a short medical leave, which skewed the results. The Six Sigma practitioner could remove those three data points from their calculations, but it would be important to note those outliers. The fact that this particular problem can happen still matters for overall process improvement. The Six Sigma team might recommend instituting a process change that addresses this issue, but it can analyze the data without those outliers to draw other conclusions.
5. The dependent variable (as described in item 1 above) needs to be normally distributed, or approximate the normal curve, within each group. In the example above, the Six Sigma team gathers data from nine employees. Within each of those nine data sets, the data needs to be normally distributed.
6. The variance within each set has to be statistically equal to the variance of the other sets — also called homogeneity of variances. The test for equal variance can be run in Minitab and will be covered later in this chapter.

After validating the assumptions and forming the hypotheses, a Six Sigma practitioner can run the one-way ANOVA manually or using statistical analysis software. In this chapter, we'll use Minitab to run the tests. When using statistical analysis software, you typically spend more time validating some of the assumptions than running the test itself.

### Running a One-Way ANOVA

To understand how to validate all the assumptions, run the one-way ANOVA, and interpret the results, consider a real-world example.

A mail-order book company wants to improve customer satisfaction with deliveries. A Six Sigma team working on the process identified packaging materials as a possible factor in customer dissatisfaction. The company currently ships books in cardboard boxes with no additional protection, which the team believes is contributing to an increase in shipment damage before it reaches the customer or when the customer opens the package.

To test that theory and pilot two proposed solutions, the team rolls out additional packaging options. Some books will ship in the regular packaging — the box with no additional material. Others will ship in boxes with packing peanuts, and still others in padded envelopes. The team rolls out the different packaging methods at three different shipping stations and logs an overall customer satisfaction score for each shipment, on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most satisfied. That data is shown below.

*(Data table: satisfaction scores from 1 to 10 for three packaging methods — Original Packaging, Padded Envelope, Packing Peanuts —, 15 samples per method.)*

To follow along with this example's one-way ANOVA, copy the data above into Minitab.

**Validate Assumptions:**

*Is the dependent variable continuous?* Yes, it's measured in interval form.

*Is the independent variable made up of two or more unrelated groups?* Yes, the independent variable is how the book is packaged.

*Is there independence of observation?* Yes, the three packaging methods have nothing to do with each other and aren't combined. The team wouldn't pack a book in a padded envelope and also put it in a box, for example.

It's worth noting here that the team rolled out the different packaging at three different stations. It would be a good idea for the team to make sure the packaging stations were treated identically in other respects, to avoid other factors influencing the pilot's outcome.

*Are there significant outliers in the data?* Graphical analysis can be an easy way to check for outliers. The boxplot (also called a box-and-whisker plot) is a good way to quickly check for outliers. Building boxplots in Minitab was covered in PART XIII, but you can run one now with the data above.

1. Click Graph > Boxplot
2. Select Multiple Ys
3. Click OK
4. Select the three data columns in the Graph Variables box
5. Click OK.

<img alt="Boxplot "Boxplot of Original Packaging, Padded Envelope, Packing Peanuts" generated by Minitab, showing the three distributions with no outliers" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


Minitab returns the chart above, which shows no outliers for any of the three data sets. What if someone, when logging customer satisfaction scores, made a mistake and entered the number 20 for one shipment? The boxplot analysis changes.

<img alt="Boxplot "Boxplot of Original Packaging, Padded Envelope, Packing Peanuts" generated by Minitab, now with an outlier flagged by an asterisk near 20 in the Packing Peanuts group" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


In the chart above, you can see an outlier point well above the box for packing peanuts. A Six Sigma practitioner reviewing this chart would spot that outlier and realize it was a measurement error — remember, the customer satisfaction scale was only supposed to go up to 10. Since there's an explanation for the outlier, it can be removed.

*Is the data in each group normal?* The fastest way to test each data set's normality is probably to run a graphical analysis in Minitab. That was also covered in PART XIII.

1. Select Stat > Basic Statistics > Graphical Summary
2. Select the first data set's column in the Variables box.
3. Make sure the confidence level is set to 95.0.
4. Click OK.

Minitab returns the following chart and data.

<img alt="Summary Report generated by Minitab for Original Packaging: histogram with fitted curve, boxplot, descriptive statistics (Mean 5,1244, StDev 0,7449, N=15), and Anderson-Darling normality test (P-Value 0,405)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The p-value for the Anderson-Darling normality test is 0.405. Remember, when testing normality, the null hypothesis is that there's no difference between the data and the normal curve. Since the p-value is above our alpha level (0.05), we fail to reject the null hypothesis — there's no evidence that the data deviates from normality.

The charts generated for the other two data sets are included below. You can see that the p-values for each also let us fail to reject the null hypothesis, which validates this assumption: there's no evidence that either group's data deviates from the normal distribution.

<img alt="Summary Report generated by Minitab for Padded Envelope: histogram with fitted curve, boxplot, descriptive statistics (Mean 5,6755, StDev 1,1386, N=15), and Anderson-Darling normality test (P-Value 0,625)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

<img alt="Summary Report generated by Minitab for Packing Peanuts: histogram with fitted curve, boxplot, descriptive statistics (Mean 7,0374, StDev 1,4858, N=15), and Anderson-Darling normality test (P-Value 0,444)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


*Is there homogeneity of variances? Are the variances between groups relatively equal?* Minitab includes an option to test for equal variances that returns two different p-values. One is the p-value for the Multiple Comparisons test, and the other is for Levene's test. Levene's test is commonly used to test equality assumptions when the data within each group is normal. That test wasn't covered earlier in PART XIII.

1. Select Stat → ANOVA → Test for Equal Variances.
2. From the dropdown, choose "Response data are in a separate column for each factor level," and select the three data columns in the Responses box.

1. Click OK.

Minitab returns an interval plot of all the data columns, along with two statistical values.

<img alt="Chart "Test for Equal Variances: Original Pac, Padded Envel, Packing Pean" generated by Minitab, with multiple-comparison intervals for the standard deviation, Multiple Comparisons P-Value 0,109 and Levene's Test P-Value 0,155" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


In the equal-variances test, you're generally concerned with Levene's test's p-value. In this case, it's above 0.05 (Minitab's default alpha setting), so you can fail to reject the null hypothesis, which is that there's no difference in variance between the data sets. In this case, even a glance at the interval plot helps you reach that conclusion. The ranges are certainly different, but the intervals aren't extremely different in length.

To consider a contrasting example, copy the following data table into Minitab.

*(Data table: two columns A and B, with 10 values each — A ranging between 4.01 and 10.00, B concentrated between 9.96 and 10.08.)*

Run the equal-variances test from the ANOVA menu using only the two data columns from the table above.

<img alt="Chart "Test for Equal Variances: A, B" generated by Minitab, showing the interval for A much wider than for B, Multiple Comparisons P-Value 0,000 and Levene's Test P-Value 0,002" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


You can quickly see these two data sets don't have equal variance. First, the intervals make that pretty obvious. The variance in set B is much smaller. Levene's test's p-value is much smaller than the alpha value, meaning you reject the null hypothesis and accept the alternative hypothesis that there's a difference in variance.

You can change the tests' alpha value under "Options," or the type of chart displayed under "Graphs," from the respective buttons in the same dialog box.

Here are the three original data sets shown via boxplot.

### Running the One-Way ANOVA Test

Now that all the assumptions have been checked, you can run the one-way ANOVA test.

Select Stat > ANOVA > One-Way. Select the dropdown option indicating the response data is in separate columns. Select the three data columns (the data for original packaging, padded envelopes, and packing peanuts) in the Responses box.

You can click Options to set the confidence interval or make sure it's still at 95%, if you'd like. Then, click OK.

Click OK in the main dialog box. Minitab will run the one-way ANOVA calculations. Depending on how much data is in the columns when you run this test, it might take a few seconds.

By default, Minitab returns two things: a graphical analysis of the data and the ANOVA results in the session window.

*(Minitab session window output: "One-way ANOVA: Original Packaging, Padded Envelope, Packing Peanuts" — Null hypothesis: All means are equal; Alternative hypothesis: At least one mean is different; Significance level α=0.05; equal variances assumed; Factor Information: 3 levels; Analysis of Variance: Factor DF=2, F-Value=9.54, P-Value=0.000; Model Summary: S=1.20581, R-sq=31.23%; Means: Original Packaging 5.133, Padded Envelope 5.667, Packing Peanuts 7.000.)*

<img alt="Interval Plot "Interval Plot of Original Pac, Padded Envel, ..." generated by Minitab, with a 95% CI for the mean of each group (Original Packaging, Padded Envelope, Packing Peanuts), showing progressively higher means" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:603px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The session window data is included above. The null hypothesis is that all the means are equal; the alternative is that at least one of the means is statistically different.

The p-value is less than the alpha value of 0.05, meaning you reject the null hypothesis and accept the alternative hypothesis that at least one of the means is different.

In business terms, the Six Sigma team now knows that "one of these things is not like the others." That can lead them to work on additional analysis or point to a problem with one or more processes. If the team was comparing average production times across several teams in the same process, it might assume the teams would complete the work in roughly equal times. If the one-way ANOVA shows that isn't true, the Six Sigma team can then ask itself: what makes this outcome statistically different? Is one team doing this better than all the others? If so, can the Six Sigma team roll that group's solutions out to the other groups? Is one team performing worse than the others? If so, what's going on with that team, and how can improvement be made?

#### Worked example on five fronts: One-Way ANOVA

Revisiting the packaging-materials example from the text above. The 45 raw values (15 per group) aren't available as text — only the summary statistics the Minitab session output reported: 3 groups of n=15, means 5.133 (Original Packaging), 5.667 (Padded Envelope), and 7.000 (Packing Peanuts), with S (pooled standard deviation) = 1.20581. It's possible to reconstruct the **entire** ANOVA from these summary statistics — that's exactly what Excel, DAX, Python, and R do below, without needing the raw data.

<img alt="Excel + Power BI (DAX) illustration of the example: 1-Way ANOVA" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: from the given means/n/S, build `MSbetween = Σnᵢ(x̄ᵢ−x̄̄)² / (k−1)` and use `MSwithin = S²` directly; `F = MSbetween/MSwithin`, and the p-value with `=F.DIST(F, k-1, N-k, TRUE)` complemented (`1-F.DIST(...)`).

**Power BI (DAX)**: a complete ANOVA (with residuals and diagnostics) isn't native in DAX (see Section 4.3) — but when you already have the means/n/S per group (as here), the F-test is a direct closed-form formula, natively computable:

```dax
F Estatistica =
VAR MediaGeral = (15*5.133 + 15*5.667 + 15*7.000) / 45
VAR QMEntre = ( 15*(5.133-MediaGeral)^2 + 15*(5.667-MediaGeral)^2 + 15*(7.000-MediaGeral)^2 ) / 2
VAR QMDentro = 1.20581 ^ 2
RETURN QMEntre / QMDentro

Valor-p = 1 - F.DIST ( [F Estatistica], 2, 42, TRUE )
```

```py-r
--- python
from scipy import stats

n = [15, 15, 15]
medias = [5.133, 5.667, 7.000]
S = 1.20581  # desvio padrao combinado (sqrt(QMdentro)) reportado pelo Minitab
k = 3
N = sum(n)

media_geral = sum(ni*mi for ni, mi in zip(n, medias)) / N
sq_entre = sum(ni*(mi-media_geral)**2 for ni, mi in zip(n, medias))
gl_entre, gl_dentro = k-1, N-k
qm_entre = sq_entre / gl_entre
qm_dentro = S**2
F = qm_entre / qm_dentro
p_valor = stats.f.sf(F, gl_entre, gl_dentro)
r2 = sq_entre / (sq_entre + qm_dentro*gl_dentro)

print(f"F = {F:.2f}   valor-p = {p_valor:.4f}   R² = {r2*100:.2f}%")
print("Decisão:", "rejeita H0 (pelo menos uma média é diferente)" if p_valor < 0.05 else "não rejeita H0")
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
n <- c(15, 15, 15)
medias <- c(5.133, 5.667, 7.000)
S <- 1.20581
k <- 3
N <- sum(n)

media_geral <- sum(n*medias) / N
sq_entre <- sum(n*(medias-media_geral)^2)
gl_entre <- k-1; gl_dentro <- N-k
qm_entre <- sq_entre / gl_entre
qm_dentro <- S^2
Fstat <- qm_entre / qm_dentro
p_valor <- pf(Fstat, gl_entre, gl_dentro, lower.tail = FALSE)
r2 <- sq_entre / (sq_entre + qm_dentro*gl_dentro)

cat(sprintf("F = %.2f   valor-p = %.4f   R2 = %.2f%%\n", Fstat, p_valor, r2*100))
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): **Stat → ANOVA → One-Way**, with the raw data in separate columns per group — reproduces the session output quoted in the text exactly (F=9.54, p-value=0.000, R²=31.23%).

*Cross-check note: all five methods converge — F ≈ 9.54, p-value ≈ 0.0004 (Minitab rounds to 0.000), and R² ≈ 31.24% — reproducing the Minitab session output numbers quoted in the text exactly (F=9.54, R-sq=31.23%), even starting from just the summary statistics.*

### What If the Variances Aren't Equal?

If you can't validate the sixth assumption about equal variances across your subgroups, you can still run a one-way ANOVA test in Minitab. Minitab uses a different statistical calculation, known as Welch's test, to provide a p-value in that case.

Use the data we found earlier with unequal variances to run this test in Minitab.

*(Same A/B data table used in the equal-variances test.)*

Select Stat > ANOVA > One-Way. Select the dropdown option indicating the response data is in separate columns. Select data columns A and B in the Responses box.

Select Options. Uncheck the "assume equal variances" box.

Click OK. Click OK again.

As in the previous example, Minitab generates both the graphical analysis and the test data in the session window.

*(Session window output: "One-way ANOVA: A, B" — equal variances NOT assumed; Welch's Test: F-Value=30.99, P-Value=0.000; Model Summary: R-sq=63.26%; Means: A N=10 Mean=6.539 StDev=1.978, B N=10 Mean=10.0221 StDev=0.0398.)*

<img alt="Interval Plot "Interval Plot of A, B" generated by Minitab, showing the 95% confidence interval for the mean of A and of B, with individual standard deviations used in the calculation" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


You can see, from Minitab's results, that equal variance wasn't assumed for this data. You also have a p-value that's effectively 0, meaning you reject the null hypothesis and accept the alternative that one of the means is statistically different: something we'd already noticed just by looking at this data's graphical interpretation earlier. As stated earlier, data doesn't always look as different when viewed graphically, which often requires statistical analysis.

### Hypothesis-Testing Assistance in Minitab

At the end of the previous unit, we noted that you can use Minitab's help menu to look up information about every function and read detailed instructions and summaries about various test types. You can also use the Minitab Assistant to help you choose a hypothesis test — including a one-way ANOVA — and run that test.

Select Assistant → Hypothesis Tests. The assistant guides your choice through questions — comparing a sample to a target, two samples against each other, or more than two samples — and, within each option, splits by data type (continuous or attribute), arriving at the right test: one-way ANOVA, standard-deviation test, chi-square, etc. Clicking the chosen test opens the corresponding dialog box, already set up and ready to use.
